newsitem.title: UK: New cocoa press said to help chocolatiers cut cost.
newsitem.headline: New cocoa press said to help chocolatiers cut cost.

text.p: Major confectioners are starting to look at a new way of processing cocoa beans that could cut processors' bills in half.

By using a screw press to extract cocoa butter and powder from the bean's nib, or the cocoa bean's inside meat, instead of a hydraulic press, "we can produce two times the volume at half the price of the conventional hydraulic press," said Rich Hollmeyer, marketing manager at Dupps USA.

Dupps, a developer and manufacturer of machinery for recycling animal proteins, ventured into cocoa processing in the early 1990s when ED & F Man Cocoa's Savannah plant in the U.S., which was then owned by Bristar, asked Dupps to develop a screw press method similar to that used to extract extra butter and powder from cocoa bean skins or nibs.

Cocoa beans are traditionally washed and winnowed to separate the skin, or hull, from the nib. Hulls are usually screw-pressed to extract additional cocoa butter and powder. The leftover hull on the screw press is discarded as animal feed.
The main products come from the nib, which is normally roasted, grinded, liquified and put through a hydraulic press to squeeze out the cocoa butter.
But after about a couple of years of research, Dupps found that by using a screw press on the nib, the roasting, grinding, liquid and hydraulic pressing steps could be eliminated.

Hollmeyer said the first Dupps machine started at the Savannah plant around 1993. Savannah's capacity is estimated near 30,000 bean tonnes. It sells most of its cocoa butter to Hershey's and its powder on the open market.

"Without the hydraulic press, capital equipment costs are cut in half because hydraulic presses are big and expensive," he said. Because roasters and grinders use a lot of energy and grinders are high maintenance, more savings are made. "There will be significant front-end capital savings."

According to figures compiled by M&M Mars, which started using Dupp's cocoa press in Indonesia for nibs late last year, costs could drop by more than half with the screw press. The figures assume processing of 10,000 bean tonnes per year with an 80-percent bean to liquid yield, 12 percent fat in powder and 54 percent fat in liquid. They do not account for installation, building, utilities and maintenance.

The savings were significant enough that Mars started to process its own beans again. Previously Mars had stopped processing its own beans and just bought cocoa butter and powder supply on the open market. Mars' Indonesia plant can process an estimated 10,000 bean tonnes.

But screw presses also have drawbacks. Purists say the roasting step is what gives beans flavour and without roasting, the end-product is flavourless. So, the machine can only be used with low-quality beans like those from Sulawesi, Indonesia. Those beans are unfermented and tend to be bland anyway.
Hollmeyer argues, though, the product can be alkalized, which changes the balance to change the bitter, acidic product to a base, which is sweet.

"It also doesn't matter as much for some confectioners because the cocoa butter is blended with other ingredients and is such a small fraction of the entire confection that it becomes a mattter of economics," he said, noting the resulting lower-grade powder can also be sold for things like cake mixes.
But Hollmeyer admitted "it's new technology for new plants. It's not for existing plants because the logistics (of integrating it) would be too difficult."
Though ED & F Man Cocoa Savannah and M&M Mars are the only firms using the screw process for nibs, Hollmeyer said other major processors worldwide have requested more information.
